learning_activity_name: Describe the concept of the atom (Dalton’s atomic theory, Bohr’s atomic theory, atomic mass and quantum theory)
sla_name: Atomic theories and the quantum model
sla_assessment_criteria: The concept of the atom is clearly described.
sla_teaching_aids: Pictures|Diagrams|Simulations|Animations or videos illustrating the structure of an atom
sla_references: TET(2023), CHEMISTRY SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Ideas about the atom developed from Dalton's solid sphere to the modern quantum model, each theory explaining more experimental facts.
sla_notes_details: Dalton's theory (1808) said that atoms are indivisible particles of an element, identical for the same element, and combine in simple whole-number ratios. Later work found subatomic particles: the electron (Thomson), the nucleus (Rutherford's gold foil experiment) and the neutron (Chadwick). Bohr's theory (1913) proposed that electrons move in fixed circular orbits with quantised energies, that no radiation is emitted in a stationary orbit, and that a photon of energy ΔE = hν is emitted or absorbed when an electron jumps between levels; it explains the line spectrum of hydrogen but fails for many-electron atoms. Quantum theory adds the wave-particle duality of de Broglie (λ = h/mv), Heisenberg's uncertainty principle and Schrödinger's wave equation, whose solutions are orbitals described by the quantum numbers n, l, ml and ms. Atomic mass is the weighted average of isotopic masses: for chlorine, 75% of Cl-35 and 25% of Cl-37 gives 35.5.
sla_notes_illustrations: The hydrogen emission line produced when an electron falls from n = 3 to n = 2 lies in the visible red region (656 nm), while transitions to n = 1 fall in the ultraviolet region (Lyman series). Boron has isotopes B-10 (20%) and B-11 (80%), so its relative atomic mass is 0.2 x 10 + 0.8 x 11 = 10.8.
sla_notes_daily_life: Neon signs, fireworks, flame colours of salts and sodium street lamps produce coloured light because electrons move between energy levels.
sla_exercise: State two postulates of Dalton's atomic theory.::All matter consists of indivisible atoms; atoms of the same element are identical and atoms combine in simple whole-number ratios.||What does the Bohr model say about the energy of an electron in an orbit?::Electron energy in a given orbit is fixed (quantised); energy is emitted or absorbed only when the electron moves between orbits.||Calculate the relative atomic mass of an element with 90% of isotope of mass 20 and 10% of mass 22.::0.90 x 20 + 0.10 x 22 = 18 + 2.2 = 20.2.

sla_teaching_aids: Pictures|Wall charts|Simulation illustrating the electronic configuration of elements
sla_references: TET(2023), CHEMISTRY SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: The arrangement of electrons in orbitals determines the chemical properties of an element and its place in the periodic table.
sla_notes_details: Electrons fill orbitals according to three rules: the Aufbau principle (lowest energy first, in the order 1s 2s 2p 3s 3p 4s 3d 4p 5s 4d 5p 6s), the Pauli exclusion principle (an orbital holds at most two electrons of opposite spin) and Hund's rule (orbitals of equal energy are filled singly with parallel spins before pairing). An s subshell has 1 orbital, p has 3, d has 5 and f has 7. Chromium (3d⁵4s¹) and copper (3d¹⁰4s¹) are exceptions because half-filled and completely filled d subshells are extra stable. Cations of the d-block lose 4s electrons before 3d electrons. Configurations can be written in full or with a noble gas core, for example [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s² for iron, and show the valence electrons that decide the group and the reactivity.
sla_notes_illustrations: Sodium (Z = 11): 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹ or [Ne] 3s¹, so it loses one electron to form Na⁺. Iron (Z = 26): [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s². Fe³⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁵, a half-filled stable configuration.
sla_notes_daily_life: The colour of gemstones such as ruby (Cr³⁺) and the magnetism of iron used in electric motors come from the electronic configuration of transition elements.
sla_exercise: Write the electronic configuration of chlorine (Z = 17).::1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁵.||State Hund's rule.::Electrons occupy degenerate orbitals singly with parallel spins before any orbital receives a second electron.||Why is the configuration of copper 3d¹⁰4s¹ and not 3d⁹4s²?::A completely filled d subshell is more stable, so one 4s electron moves into the 3d subshell.

sla_method: Hands-on experience activities and Group discussion

sla_teaching_aids: Molecular models|Pictures|Local materials|Video showing interactions of atoms
sla_references: TET(2023), CHEMISTRY SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Atoms join by bonds to reach stable electron arrangements, and the type of bond determines the properties of a substance.
sla_notes_details: Ionic bonding is the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions formed by electron transfer, giving high melting points and conduction when molten. Covalent bonding is the sharing of electron pairs; dative (coordinate) bonds arise when both electrons come from one atom, as in NH₄⁺. Sigma bonds are formed by head-on overlap and pi bonds by sideways overlap of p orbitals; hybridisation (sp, sp², sp³) explains the linear, trigonal planar and tetrahedral shapes of BeCl₂, BF₃ and CH₄. Valence shell electron pair repulsion (VSEPR) predicts shapes: NH₃ is pyramidal (107°) and H₂O bent (104.5°) because lone pairs repel more strongly. Bond polarity depends on electronegativity difference; intermolecular forces include London dispersion, dipole-dipole and hydrogen bonding, which explains the high boiling point of water. Metallic bonding is a lattice of cations in a sea of delocalised electrons.
sla_notes_illustrations: In CH₄, carbon mixes one 2s and three 2p orbitals into four sp³ orbitals directed to the corners of a tetrahedron, giving 109.5° angles. Ethene has a C=C made of one sigma and one pi bond with sp² carbon atoms and 120° angles.
sla_notes_daily_life: Table salt dissolves and conducts as ions, sugar melts easily because of weak forces, diamond is very hard because of covalent networks and copper wires conduct because of delocalised electrons.
sla_exercise: Distinguish a sigma bond from a pi bond.::A sigma bond is formed by head-on overlap of orbitals along the bond axis; a pi bond is formed by sideways overlap of p orbitals above and below the axis.||Predict the shape of the ammonia molecule and explain.::Pyramidal, because the nitrogen has three bond pairs and one lone pair, and the lone pair repels the bond pairs (angle about 107°).||Why does water have a higher boiling point than hydrogen sulphide?::Water molecules form strong hydrogen bonds, which need more energy to break.

sla_assessment_criteria: The concept of gases in terms of gas laws and the kinetic theory of gases is clearly described.
sla_teaching_aids: Diagrams|Pictures|Wall charts|Simulations|Videos illustrating gas laws|Kinetic theory of gases balloons|Pollen grains|Water|Light source|Microscope|Thermometer|Bicycle pump|Heat source|Bicycle tyres
sla_references: TET(2023), CHEMISTRY SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: The gas laws relate pressure, volume, temperature and amount of gas, and the kinetic theory explains them at the molecular level.
sla_notes_details: Boyle's law: PV = constant at constant temperature. Charles's law: V/T = constant at constant pressure with T in kelvin. Pressure law: P/T = constant at constant volume. Combined: P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂, and Avogadro's law says equal volumes of gases at the same conditions contain equal numbers of molecules. The ideal gas equation is PV = nRT with R = 8.314 J/mol K. Dalton's law states that the total pressure is the sum of the partial pressures, and Graham's law states that the rate of diffusion is inversely proportional to the square root of the molar mass. The kinetic theory assumes that gas molecules are in random motion, have negligible volume, no attractive forces and elastic collisions, and that the average kinetic energy is proportional to the absolute temperature. Real gases deviate from ideal behaviour at high pressure and low temperature, and the van der Waals equation (P + a n²/V²)(V - nb) = nRT corrects for this.
sla_notes_illustrations: A 2.0 dm³ gas at 100 kPa and 27 °C is heated to 127 °C at constant pressure: V₂ = 2.0 x 400/300 = 2.67 dm³. The volume of 1 mol at s.t.p. is 22.4 dm³, and hydrogen diffuses 4 times faster than oxygen since √(32/2) = 4.
sla_notes_daily_life: Inflating a tyre, breathing, the working of a syringe, the smell of cooking spreading through a house and the fizzing of a soda bottle are everyday gas-law events.
sla_exercise: State Boyle's law.::At constant temperature, the volume of a fixed mass of gas is inversely proportional to its pressure.||A gas occupies 500 cm³ at 2.0 atm. What volume does it occupy at 4.0 atm and the same temperature?::V = 2.0 x 500/4.0 = 250 cm³.||Find the number of moles of gas in 5.0 dm³ at 200 kPa and 300 K (R = 8.314).::n = PV/RT = 200 000 x 0.0050 / (8.314 x 300) = 0.40 mol.

sla_assessment_criteria: Applications of gas laws in daily life are realised.

sla_references: TET(2023), CHEMISTRY SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Understanding gas laws explains the design and safe use of many household and industrial products.
sla_notes_details: In a fire extinguisher, carbon dioxide is stored under high pressure and expands when released, cooling and smothering the fire, as in Boyle's law and Joule-Thomson cooling. Aerosol cans contain a propellant gas at pressure that pushes the liquid out; heating them raises pressure (P/T constant) and can cause explosions. Tyres are inflated by reducing volume of air (Boyle's law) and pressure rises after long journeys because temperature increases. Baking depends on the release of CO₂ from baking powder, which expands in the hot oven (Charles's law) and makes dough rise. Gases are liquefied by compression and cooling below the critical temperature, for example LPG for cooking and liquid nitrogen for preserving. Helium balloons rise because helium is less dense than air (M = 4 against 29 g/mol).
sla_notes_illustrations: If a car tyre is filled to 220 kPa at 27 °C and reaches 47 °C during a trip, the pressure becomes 220 x 320/300 = 235 kPa at constant volume, which is why tyre pressure is checked when the tyre is cold.
sla_notes_daily_life: Cooking with LPG cylinders, using spray perfumes and insecticides, filling bicycle tyres and floating helium balloons at parties all apply these gas laws.
sla_exercise: Why should aerosol cans not be heated or thrown into fire?::Heating increases the gas pressure inside (P proportional to T) and the can may burst.||Explain how baking powder makes a cake rise.::It releases carbon dioxide, which expands when heated in the oven and forms bubbles that raise the dough.||Why is LPG stored as a liquid in cylinders?::Compression and cooling turn it into liquid, so a large amount can be stored in a small volume.

sla_name: Periodic trends of elements
sla_assessment_criteria: Periodic trends of elements in the modern periodic table are well described.
sla_teaching_aids: Pictures|Wall charts of modern periodic table|Graphics programme demonstrating periodic trends of elements
sla_references: TET(2023), CHEMISTRY SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: The properties of elements change in a regular way across a period and down a group of the modern periodic table.
sla_notes_details: Atomic radius decreases across a period because increasing nuclear charge attracts electrons more strongly while shielding remains almost the same, and increases down a group as extra shells are added. First ionisation energy generally increases across a period and decreases down a group, with dips at Group 3 (start of a new p subshell) and Group 6 (paired electrons repel). Electron affinity is the energy released when a gaseous atom gains an electron and is most negative for halogens. Electronegativity, on the Pauling scale, increases across a period and decreases down a group, with fluorine highest at 4.0. Metallic character decreases across a period and increases down a group, and melting points rise from Na to a maximum at Si (giant covalent structure) and then fall sharply for the simple molecules of P, S, Cl and Ar.
sla_notes_illustrations: In Period 3, atomic radius falls from Na (186 pm) to Cl (99 pm), while first ionisation energy rises from 496 kJ/mol (Na) to 1251 kJ/mol (Cl) with a small drop from Mg to Al. Down Group 1, Li has 520 kJ/mol but Cs only 376 kJ/mol.
sla_notes_daily_life: Choosing sodium or potassium for salts in fertilizers, using chlorine for water treatment and picking metals for wires or batteries depend on these trends.
sla_exercise: State the trend in atomic radius across Period 3 and explain it.::It decreases because nuclear charge increases while electrons enter the same shell, so the electrons are pulled closer.||Why is the first ionisation energy of aluminium lower than that of magnesium?::The outer electron of Al is in a higher-energy 3p orbital, which is further from the nucleus and shielded by the 3s electrons, so it is removed more easily.||Which element has the highest electronegativity?::Fluorine.

sla_notes_intro: Periodic trends can be used to predict and explain the behaviour of oxides, chlorides, hydrides and reactions of elements.
sla_notes_details: Reaction with water: sodium reacts vigorously with cold water to give NaOH and hydrogen, magnesium reacts slowly with cold water but quickly with steam, and aluminium is protected by an oxide layer. Oxides change from basic (Na₂O, MgO) through amphoteric (Al₂O₃) to acidic (SiO₂, P₄O₁₀, SO₂, Cl₂O₇); solutions of the oxides have pH values that change from strongly alkaline to strongly acidic. Chlorides of Na and Mg are ionic and dissolve in water without hydrolysis, AlCl₃ is partly covalent and hydrolyses, and SiCl₄ and PCl₅ hydrolyse completely giving acidic solutions. Hydrides of Group 1 and 2 are ionic and hydrides of Groups 14 to 17 are covalent, with stability decreasing down a group. Trends are supported by experiments and data such as electrical conductivity and pH.
sla_notes_illustrations: Adding sodium oxide to water gives NaOH with pH 14, whereas P₄O₁₀ gives H₃PO₄ with pH about 1: Na₂O + H₂O → 2NaOH and P₄O₁₀ + 6H₂O → 4H₃PO₄.
sla_notes_daily_life: Antacids use basic oxides and hydroxides of magnesium and aluminium, while acid rain is caused by acidic oxides of sulphur and nitrogen.
sla_exercise: Write the equation for the reaction of sodium with water.::2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂.||What type of oxide is aluminium oxide? Give one equation.::Amphoteric: Al₂O₃ + 6HCl → 2AlCl₃ + 3H₂O and Al₂O₃ + 2NaOH + 3H₂O → 2Na[Al(OH)₄].||Why does the acidity of the oxides increase across Period 3?::Metallic character decreases and non-metallic character increases, so the oxides change from ionic and basic to covalent and acidic.

sla_name: Colligative properties of solutions
sla_assessment_criteria: Colligative properties are correctly described.
sla_teaching_aids: Thermometer|Beaker|Common salt|Table sugar|Weighing bottle|Beckman’s apparatus|Landsberger apparatus osmometer|Plastic bottle|Analytical balance|Freezing point apparatus|Ethyl glycol|Coolants|Video showing colligative properties
sla_references: TET(2023), CHEMISTRY SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Colligative properties depend on the number of solute particles in a solution and not on their nature.
sla_notes_details: Relative lowering of vapour pressure equals the mole fraction of solute (Raoult's law): (P° - P)/P° = x_solute. Boiling point elevation is ΔTb = Kb m and freezing point depression is ΔTf = Kf m, where m is the molality; for water Kb = 0.52 and Kf = 1.86 K kg/mol. Osmotic pressure is π = cRT (van't Hoff). For electrolytes the van't Hoff factor i (for example 2 for NaCl) multiplies the effect. These properties are used to find molar masses: M = Kf x mass of solute / (ΔTf x kg of solvent). Ideal solutions obey Raoult's law, while non-ideal solutions show positive or negative deviation according to intermolecular interactions.
sla_notes_illustrations: Dissolving 18 g of glucose (M = 180) in 500 g of water gives molality 0.20 mol/kg, so ΔTf = 1.86 x 0.20 = 0.37 K and the freezing point is -0.37 °C. The osmotic pressure of 0.10 mol/dm³ glucose at 300 K is 0.10 x 8.314 x 300 = 249 kPa (with concentration in mol/m³).
sla_notes_daily_life: Salt on icy roads, antifreeze in car radiators, cooking food in salted water and the osmosis of water into plant roots involve colligative properties.
sla_exercise: List four colligative properties.::Lowering of vapour pressure, elevation of boiling point, depression of freezing point and osmotic pressure.||Calculate the boiling point elevation when 0.50 mol of sugar is dissolved in 1.0 kg of water (Kb = 0.52).::ΔTb = 0.52 x 0.50 = 0.26 K.||Why does 0.1 mol/kg NaCl lower the freezing point about twice as much as 0.1 mol/kg glucose?::NaCl dissociates into two ions (i = 2), producing twice as many particles.

sla_notes_intro: Colligative properties are used in purification, medicine, food preservation and engineering.
sla_notes_details: In reverse osmosis a pressure greater than the osmotic pressure is applied to salty water so that pure water passes through a semipermeable membrane, giving desalinated drinking water. Dialysis in kidney machines lets waste such as urea pass through a membrane from blood into dialysis fluid while keeping proteins and blood cells. Food is preserved with high concentrations of salt or sugar (as in jam, salted fish) that lower water activity and draw water out of microbes by osmosis, so they cannot grow. Antifreeze (ethylene glycol) lowers the freezing point and raises the boiling point of engine coolant, and salt is spread on roads to melt ice. Intravenous fluids are made isotonic (0.9% saline) so that red blood cells do not shrink or burst.
sla_notes_illustrations: A 30% ethylene glycol solution in a car radiator freezes near -15 °C and boils near 104 °C, protecting the engine in both cold and hot conditions. Placing red blood cells in 5% salt solution makes them shrink (crenation) as water leaves them.
sla_notes_daily_life: Drying fish with salt, making jam, using saline drips in hospitals, water purification with reverse osmosis and antifreeze in vehicles all use colligative properties.
sla_exercise: How does salt preserve fish?::The high salt concentration draws water out of bacteria by osmosis, so they cannot grow.||What is meant by an isotonic solution?::A solution having the same osmotic pressure as body fluids such as blood.||State the principle of reverse osmosis.::Applying pressure greater than the osmotic pressure forces solvent to move from the concentrated to the dilute side through a semipermeable membrane.

sla_notes_intro: Mixtures of two liquids may be immiscible, partially miscible or completely miscible, and a solute can distribute itself between two solvents.
sla_notes_details: Immiscible liquids such as water and hexane form two layers and each exerts its own vapour pressure, so the mixture boils below the boiling point of either liquid (steam distillation); the total pressure is P = P₁° + P₂° and the mole ratio in the vapour is n₁/n₂ = P₁°/P₂°. Completely miscible liquids form ideal solutions following Raoult's law (benzene and toluene) or non-ideal ones with maximum or minimum boiling azeotropes (ethanol and water, 95.6% ethanol) that cannot be separated fully by fractional distillation. The Nernst distribution law states that at constant temperature a solute distributes between two immiscible solvents so that the ratio of concentrations is constant: K_D = C₁/C₂. Extraction is more efficient when the solvent is used in several small portions than in one large portion.
sla_notes_illustrations: Iodine has K_D = 85 between CCl₄ and water. Shaking 100 cm³ of aqueous iodine with 10 cm³ of CCl₄ extracts a fraction 85 x 10/(85 x 10 + 100) = 0.89 of the iodine in one step.
sla_notes_daily_life: Extracting essential oils from lemongrass by steam distillation, removing caffeine from coffee and separating oil from water use these principles.
sla_exercise: State the distribution law.::At constant temperature, a solute distributes itself between two immiscible solvents so that the ratio of its concentrations in the two solvents is constant.||Why does a mixture of two immiscible liquids boil at a lower temperature than either liquid?::Each liquid exerts its own vapour pressure, so the total vapour pressure reaches atmospheric pressure at a lower temperature.||Why can ethanol and water not be completely separated by fractional distillation?::They form an azeotrope of constant boiling composition (about 95.6% ethanol) which distils without change of composition.

sla_notes_intro: Liquid-liquid systems are used in industry to extract, separate and purify useful substances.
sla_notes_details: Pharmaceutical industries use solvent extraction to isolate drugs such as quinine and artemisinin from plant materials using solvents like ethanol or ether in which the compound is more soluble than in water. Steam distillation separates temperature-sensitive substances such as essential oils (clove, eucalyptus) that would decompose at their normal boiling points. Fractional distillation separates crude oil into petrol, kerosene and diesel and ethanol from fermentation mixtures. Partition chromatography, based on distribution of substances between a stationary and a mobile phase, purifies and identifies compounds such as amino acids, pigments and drug residues. Repeated extraction with small volumes of solvent gives better recovery, as shown by the distribution law.
sla_notes_illustrations: To extract clove oil, crushed cloves are heated with steam; the oil vaporises together with steam at about 100 °C instead of its normal boiling point of 250 °C, then condenses and separates from water in a separating funnel.
sla_notes_daily_life: Making herbal medicines, perfumes and flavourings, decaffeinating tea and refining fuels use these separation techniques.
sla_exercise: Name the technique used to obtain clove oil from cloves.::Steam distillation.||Why is extraction with two 50 cm³ portions of solvent better than one 100 cm³ portion?::More solute is removed because each fresh portion re-establishes the distribution equilibrium.||Give one pharmaceutical application of solvent extraction.::Extracting quinine from cinchona bark or artemisinin from Artemisia leaves.

sla_teaching_aids: Salts|Acid|Base|Thermometer|Analytical balance|Magnesium ribbon|Sodium thiosulphate|Calorimeters|Chemical indicators|Simulation|Illustrating energetics

sla_notes_intro: Energetics studies the heat energy changes accompanying chemical reactions.
sla_notes_details: Enthalpy change ΔH is the heat exchanged at constant pressure: negative for exothermic and positive for endothermic reactions. Standard enthalpies are defined at 298 K and 100 kPa: formation ΔHf°, combustion ΔHc°, neutralisation and atomisation. Heat is measured with a calorimeter using q = mcΔT. Hess's law states that the enthalpy change of a reaction is independent of the route taken, so ΔH can be found from cycles: ΔH°reaction = ΣΔHf°(products) - ΣΔHf°(reactants) or from combustion data, ΔH = ΣΔHc(reactants) - ΣΔHc(products). Bond enthalpy estimates give ΔH = Σ(bonds broken) - Σ(bonds formed). The Born-Haber cycle applies Hess's law to lattice energy. Spontaneity depends on ΔG = ΔH - TΔS.
sla_notes_illustrations: For C(s) + O₂ → CO₂ ΔH = -394 kJ and for CO + ½O₂ → CO₂ ΔH = -283 kJ, the enthalpy of formation of CO from C + ½O₂ is -394 - (-283) = -111 kJ/mol. Burning 0.50 g of ethanol raises 200 g of water by 15 K: q = 200 x 4.18 x 15 = 12.5 kJ.
sla_notes_daily_life: Comparing the energy content of fuels such as charcoal, gas and kerosene, and understanding heat released by neutralising acids, use enthalpy changes.
sla_exercise: State Hess's law.::The total enthalpy change of a reaction is the same regardless of the route by which the reaction occurs.||Calculate the heat needed to raise 250 g of water from 20 °C to 60 °C (c = 4.18 J/g K).::q = 250 x 4.18 x 40 = 41 800 J = 41.8 kJ.||Distinguish exothermic from endothermic reactions.::An exothermic reaction releases heat (ΔH negative); an endothermic reaction absorbs heat (ΔH positive).

sla_notes_intro: Enthalpy changes explain the energy from fuels, cooking and food in the human body.
sla_notes_details: Fuels are compared by the enthalpy of combustion per gram: hydrogen releases about 142 kJ/g, methane 55 kJ/g, petrol 46 kJ/g, ethanol 30 kJ/g and wood about 16 kJ/g. Complete combustion releases more energy than incomplete combustion, which forms CO and carbon and is dangerous. In cooking, chemical energy from gas or charcoal is transferred to food as heat, and efficient stoves reduce heat loss. In the body, metabolism of glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O, ΔH = -2803 kJ/mol, releases energy stepwise so that about 40% is stored as ATP and the remainder maintains body temperature. Energy values of food are found by calorimetry: carbohydrates and proteins give about 17 kJ/g and fats 37 kJ/g. Cold packs use endothermic dissolving of ammonium nitrate and hot packs use exothermic reactions.
sla_notes_illustrations: Burning 1 mol of methane releases 890 kJ, so 16 g gives 890 kJ (55.6 kJ/g), whereas 1 mol of ethanol (46 g) gives 1367 kJ (29.7 kJ/g); methane is therefore a better fuel by mass.
sla_notes_daily_life: Choosing LPG or charcoal for cooking, understanding why athletes need energy-rich food and why fats give more energy than sugar are practical applications.
sla_exercise: Write an equation for the complete combustion of methane.::CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O.||Why is incomplete combustion of fuel undesirable?::It releases less energy and produces poisonous carbon monoxide and soot.||Why do fats provide more energy per gram than carbohydrates?::Fats are more reduced (contain more C-H bonds and less oxygen), so more energy is released on oxidation.

sla_notes_intro: This topic introduces the main families of organic compounds beyond alkanes and alkenes: arenes, haloalkanes, phenols, carbonyl compounds, carboxylic acids, amines and polymers.
sla_notes_details: Benzene, C₆H₆, has a planar ring of six sp² carbons with delocalised π electrons giving stability, so it undergoes substitution rather than addition. Haloalkanes (R-X) have a polar C-X bond and undergo nucleophilic substitution and elimination. Phenols have -OH on a benzene ring, are weakly acidic and give a violet colour with FeCl₃. Carbonyl compounds contain C=O: aldehydes (RCHO) are oxidised easily while ketones (RCOR') are not. Carboxylic acids (RCOOH) are weak acids that form esters, amides and acyl chlorides. Amines (RNH₂) are organic bases with a lone pair on nitrogen. Polymers are large molecules formed from monomers by addition (poly(ethene)) or condensation (nylon, polyester). Some, such as polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, carbonyl compounds and vinyl chloride, are hazardous to health.
sla_notes_illustrations: Ethanal, CH₃CHO, is an aldehyde and propanone, CH₃COCH₃, a ketone; Tollens' reagent gives a silver mirror with ethanal but not with propanone. Benzoic acid, C₆H₅COOH, is an aromatic carboxylic acid used as a food preservative.
sla_notes_daily_life: Aspirin, paracetamol, plastics, detergents, pesticides, fragrances, vinegar and dyes are all made from these compounds.
sla_exercise: Why does benzene undergo substitution rather than addition reactions?::Its delocalised π electron system is very stable and addition would destroy it.||Give a test that distinguishes an aldehyde from a ketone.::Tollens' reagent gives a silver mirror (or Fehling's gives a red precipitate) with an aldehyde but not with a ketone.||Name one health hazard of polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons.::Some, such as benzo[a]pyrene from smoke and grilled food, are carcinogenic.

sla_notes_intro: IUPAC rules give each organic compound a unique systematic name based on its structure.
sla_notes_details: The steps are to find the longest carbon chain containing the principal functional group, number it from the end that gives the lowest number to the principal group, name and number substituents alphabetically, and use prefixes di-, tri- for repeated groups. Suffixes show the group: -al (aldehyde), -one (ketone), -oic acid (carboxylic acid), -oate (ester), -amine (amine), -ol (alcohol). Halogens are named as prefixes: chloro-, bromo-. Benzene compounds are named as derivatives such as nitrobenzene, methylbenzene (toluene), phenol, benzoic acid and benzaldehyde; positions on the ring are numbered 1,2 (ortho), 1,3 (meta) or 1,4 (para). Priority order of principal groups is acid > ester > amide > aldehyde > ketone > alcohol > amine.
sla_notes_illustrations: CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂COOH is 3-methylbutanoic acid; CH₃CHBrCH₃ is 2-bromopropane; CH₃CH₂CHO is propanal; C₆H₅OH is phenol; and CH₃-C₆H₄-Cl with groups on positions 1 and 4 is 1-chloro-4-methylbenzene.
sla_notes_daily_life: Correct names are needed on medicine labels, pesticide packs and safety data sheets so that people avoid confusing similar chemicals.

sla_notes_intro: Reactions of aromatic compounds, phenols, carbonyl compounds and carboxylic acids are used to make useful consumer products.
sla_notes_details: Benzene undergoes electrophilic substitution: nitration with concentrated HNO₃/H₂SO₄ gives nitrobenzene, halogenation with Cl₂/FeCl₃ gives chlorobenzene, and Friedel-Crafts alkylation with RCl/AlCl₃ gives alkylbenzenes. Phenol reacts with bromine water to give a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol and with NaOH to form sodium phenoxide. Aldehydes and ketones undergo nucleophilic addition with HCN and are reduced by NaBH₄ or LiAlH₄ to alcohols; aldehydes are oxidised to carboxylic acids. Carboxylic acids react with alcohols in the presence of concentrated H₂SO₄ to form esters (fragrances), and saponification of fats and oils (triglycerides) with NaOH or KOH gives soap and glycerol. Pesticides such as DDT and chlorophenoxy herbicides are made from chlorinated aromatic compounds, while esters give perfumes with fruit smells.
sla_notes_illustrations: Saponification: fat + 3NaOH → 3 sodium stearate (soap) + glycerol. Esterification: CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH ⇌ CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O gives ethyl ethanoate with a fruity smell.
sla_notes_daily_life: Soap making from oils, perfume production from flowers and orange peels, and the use of pesticides on crops apply these reactions.
sla_exercise: Write an equation for the formation of ethyl ethanoate.::CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH ⇌ CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O (concentrated H₂SO₄ catalyst).||What is saponification?::The alkaline hydrolysis of fats or oils by NaOH or KOH to form soap and glycerol.||What is observed when bromine water is added to phenol?::The orange colour disappears and a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol forms.

sla_notes_intro: Haloalkanes, amines and polymers take part in reactions that produce plastics, dyes, detergents and rubber.
sla_notes_details: Haloalkanes undergo nucleophilic substitution with OH⁻ to give alcohols, with NH₃ to give amines and with CN⁻ to lengthen a chain, and elimination with alcoholic KOH to give alkenes. Primary amines are prepared by reducing nitro compounds or nitriles, and aromatic amines (phenylamine) are diazotised at 0-5 °C with NaNO₂/HCl to form diazonium salts that couple with phenols to make azo dyes. Addition polymerisation of alkenes gives poly(ethene), poly(chloroethene) (PVC) and polystyrene; condensation polymerisation of diamines with diacids gives nylon and of diols with diacids gives polyesters such as Terylene. Natural rubber is a polymer of isoprene and vulcanisation with sulphur cross-links chains to make it stronger. Detergents are synthetic surfactants made from sulphonation of alkylbenzenes followed by neutralisation.
sla_notes_illustrations: Nylon-6,6 forms from hexane-1,6-diamine and hexanedioic acid with loss of water at each amide link. The reaction of benzenediazonium chloride with phenol in alkaline solution at 5 °C gives an orange-red azo dye.
sla_notes_daily_life: Plastic bags, PVC pipes, nylon ropes and clothes, tyres, dyes for textiles and washing powders all come from these reactions, and their disposal needs careful recycling.
sla_exercise: Name the type of reaction of a haloalkane with aqueous KOH.::Nucleophilic substitution, giving an alcohol.||Write the monomer of poly(chloroethene).::Chloroethene, CH₂=CHCl.||Why must diazotisation be carried out at 0-5 °C?::Diazonium salts decompose at higher temperatures.

sla_notes_intro: Synthesis in the laboratory shows how starting materials are converted step by step into new organic products.
sla_notes_details: A synthesis plans the route, selects reagents and conditions, carries out the reaction, and then separates and purifies the product by filtration, recrystallisation, distillation or solvent extraction, and identifies it by melting point, boiling point and simple tests. Examples include nitrobenzene from benzene by nitration at below 55 °C, phenylamine by reduction of nitrobenzene with tin and HCl, aspirin by acetylation of salicylic acid with ethanoic anhydride, soap by boiling oil with NaOH followed by salting out, and nylon by interfacial polymerisation of a diamine and diacid chloride. Percentage yield is (actual yield / theoretical yield) x 100. Safety requires fume cupboards, eye protection, careful heating and correct disposal of solvents and waste.
sla_notes_illustrations: In making aspirin, 2.0 g salicylic acid (M = 138) gives a theoretical 2.61 g of aspirin (M = 180). If 2.0 g is obtained, the percentage yield is 2.0/2.61 x 100 = 77%. Recrystallisation from hot ethanol/water removes impurities and a melting point of 135 °C indicates pure aspirin.
sla_notes_daily_life: Small industries make soaps, candles, perfumes and dyes using the same steps: reaction, separation, purification and testing of the product.
sla_exercise: What is percentage yield?::The ratio of actual yield to theoretical yield expressed as a percentage.||Why is the product of a synthesis recrystallised?::To remove impurities so that the product is purer and has a sharp melting point.||Name the reactants used to prepare aspirin.::Salicylic acid and ethanoic anhydride, with an acid catalyst.

sla_notes_details: Students identify a problem, review literature, state the objectives and hypothesis, plan the materials, methods, safety and budget, and start collecting data. sla_notes_intro: A reversible reaction reaches a dynamic equilibrium, where the forward and backward rates are equal and the concentrations stay constant.
sla_notes_details: For aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD, the equilibrium constant is Kc = [C]^c[D]^d / [A]^a[B]^b, and for gases Kp uses partial pressures, with Kp = Kc(RT)^Δn. Le Chatelier's principle predicts the shift of equilibrium: adding reactant or removing product shifts it right, increasing pressure favours the side with fewer gas moles, and raising temperature favours the endothermic direction; only temperature changes the value of K, and a catalyst speeds up both rates equally. Comparing the reaction quotient Q with K shows the direction of change. Ionic equilibria include solubility products, Ksp = [M⁺][A⁻] for a sparingly soluble salt, and the common ion effect. Acid-base equilibria use Ka = [H⁺][A⁻]/[HA], pH = -log[H⁺], Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻] = 1.0 x 10⁻¹⁴ at 25 °C, and buffers follow pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]).
sla_notes_illustrations: For N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, if equilibrium concentrations are 0.50, 1.5 and 0.20 mol/dm³, Kc = 0.20²/(0.50 x 1.5³) = 0.024. A 0.10 mol/dm³ ethanoic acid (Ka = 1.8 x 10⁻⁵) has [H⁺] = √(1.8 x 10⁻⁶) = 1.3 x 10⁻³, pH = 2.9. The esterification CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH ⇌ CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O is another example.
sla_notes_daily_life: Blood is buffered at pH 7.4, antacids shift equilibria in the stomach and the Haber process for fertilizers is designed using equilibrium principles.
sla_exercise: State Le Chatelier's principle.::When a system at equilibrium is disturbed, it adjusts to partly oppose the disturbance and restores equilibrium.||Write the Kc expression for 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃.::Kc = [SO₃]² / ([SO₂]²[O₂]).||Calculate the pH of a 0.010 mol/dm³ solution of HCl.::pH = -log(0.010) = 2.

sla_notes_intro: Laboratory work on equilibria includes preparing buffers, titrating acids with bases and measuring equilibrium constants.
sla_notes_details: A buffer is prepared by mixing a weak acid with its salt, for example 0.10 mol/dm³ ethanoic acid with 0.10 mol/dm³ sodium ethanoate (pH ≈ 4.76), and its stability is tested by adding small amounts of acid or base and measuring pH with a pH meter. In an acid-base titration a burette delivers a standard solution into a measured volume in a conical flask with a suitable indicator: methyl orange for strong acid-weak base, phenolphthalein for weak acid-strong base, and either for strong-strong. The concentration follows from M₁V₁/n₁ = M₂V₂/n₂. Titration curves show the equivalence point and a half-equivalence point where pH = pKa. Kc for esterification can be found by titrating the remaining acid. Results are recorded in tables with concordant titres (within 0.10 cm³), analysed and reported with sources of error.
sla_notes_illustrations: 25.0 cm³ of NaOH is neutralised by 20.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol/dm³ HCl, so [NaOH] = 0.100 x 20.0 / 25.0 = 0.0800 mol/dm³. Adding 1 cm³ of 0.1 mol/dm³ HCl to 100 cm³ of the buffer changes pH by only about 0.01 unit, but changes pure water from pH 7 to pH 3.
sla_notes_daily_life: Quality control in food, water and pharmaceutical laboratories uses titration and buffers to measure acidity and keep products stable.
sla_exercise: Which indicator suits a titration of ethanoic acid with sodium hydroxide?::Phenolphthalein, because the equivalence point is above pH 7.||15.0 cm³ of H₂SO₄ is neutralised by 30.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol/dm³ NaOH. Find the concentration of the acid.::H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O; moles NaOH = 0.00300, so moles acid = 0.00150 and concentration = 0.00150/0.0150 = 0.100 mol/dm³.||What is a buffer solution?::A solution that resists changes in pH when small amounts of acid or alkali are added, usually a weak acid and its salt.

sla_notes_intro: Equilibrium principles guide the choice of conditions in industrial processes and explain natural systems.
sla_notes_details: In the Haber process N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ (ΔH = -92 kJ), high pressure (about 200 atm) increases yield, a moderate temperature of about 450 °C balances yield and rate, and an iron catalyst speeds up reaching equilibrium; unreacted gases are recycled. The Contact process for H₂SO₄ uses 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃ with V₂O₅ catalyst at 450 °C and 1-2 atm, because the yield is already about 99%, and SO₃ is absorbed in concentrated H₂SO₄. Fertilizers such as ammonium nitrate and urea depend on ammonia. Photochromic lenses contain silver chloride in equilibrium 2AgCl ⇌ 2Ag + Cl₂ that darkens in sunlight and reverses in the dark. Acids, bases and salts in food industries control taste and preservation, for example citric acid, benzoate preservatives and sodium bicarbonate. In nature the CO₂/HCO₃⁻ buffer keeps ocean and blood pH stable.
sla_notes_illustrations: For the Haber process, raising the pressure from 1 atm to 200 atm increases ammonia percentage from about 0.5% to more than 30% at 450 °C. Cooling the reaction mixture to condense NH₃ removes product and shifts the equilibrium right.
sla_notes_daily_life: Fertilizers for crops, batteries acid for vehicles, sodium bicarbonate in baking, sunglasses that darken and food preservatives rely on equilibrium chemistry.
sla_exercise: Why is a high pressure used in the Haber process?::The forward reaction reduces the number of gas moles (4 to 2), so high pressure shifts the equilibrium towards ammonia.||Why is a very high temperature not used in the Haber process?::The reaction is exothermic, so high temperature lowers the yield of ammonia.||Give one use of sulphuric acid.::Making fertilizers such as ammonium sulphate, or lead-acid batteries and detergents.

sla_notes_intro: Transition elements are d-block metals whose partly filled d orbitals give them special properties.
sla_notes_details: A transition element forms at least one ion with a partly filled d subshell; scandium and zinc are therefore not typical. Their common properties are variable oxidation states because 4s and 3d electrons have similar energies (Mn shows +2 to +7), formation of coloured compounds because d-d electronic transitions absorb visible light (Cu²⁺ blue, Fe³⁺ yellow-brown, MnO₄⁻ purple), catalytic activity (Fe in the Haber process, V₂O₅ in the Contact process, MnO₂ in decomposition of H₂O₂), paramagnetism due to unpaired electrons, high melting points and densities, and formation of alloys and complex ions. Trends across the first row include gradual changes in atomic radius and ionisation energy because the added 3d electrons shield the 4s electrons only slightly. Redox chemistry of manganese and iron is used in titrations with KMnO₄.
sla_notes_illustrations: MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5Fe²⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5Fe³⁺ + 4H₂O; in this titration the purple permanganate is decolourised until the endpoint, when a faint pink persists. Vanadium shows +2 (violet), +3 (green), +4 (blue) and +5 (yellow) states when reduced with zinc.
sla_notes_daily_life: Steel and stainless steel, coloured pottery glazes, paints, batteries, catalytic converters in cars and iron in hemoglobin all use transition elements.
sla_exercise: Why is zinc not regarded as a transition element?::Its Zn²⁺ ion has a completely filled 3d¹⁰ subshell, so it has no partly filled d subshell.||Explain why transition metal compounds are usually coloured.::Electrons absorb certain wavelengths of visible light in d-d transitions between split d orbitals, and the transmitted colour is seen.||Name two transition metals used as catalysts and the process.::Iron in the Haber process and vanadium(V) oxide in the Contact process.

sla_notes_intro: A complex has a central metal ion bonded to ligands by dative covalent bonds.
sla_notes_details: Ligands donate lone pairs: monodentate (H₂O, NH₃, Cl⁻, CN⁻), bidentate (ethane-1,2-diamine, oxalate) and polydentate (EDTA⁴⁻). The coordination number is the number of donor atoms bonded to the metal, commonly 2 (linear, [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺), 4 (tetrahedral [CuCl₄]²⁻ or square planar [Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂]) and 6 (octahedral [Fe(CN)₆]³⁻). Naming follows IUPAC: ligands alphabetically, then the metal with oxidation state in Roman numerals, e.g. hexaamminecobalt(III) chloride. Isomerism can be geometric (cis and trans) or optical. Factors affecting complex formation are the charge and size of the metal ion, the nature of the ligand and the availability of empty orbitals. Crystal field theory explains that the d orbitals split in energy (Δ) and that the size of Δ decides colour and magnetic properties.
sla_notes_illustrations: In [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ the copper(II) ion has coordination number 6 and a charge of +2. In [Fe(CN)₆]³⁻ the oxidation state of iron is +3 because 6(-1) + x = -3. Cisplatin, cis-[Pt(NH₃)₂Cl₂], is a square planar drug for cancer.
sla_notes_daily_life: Haemoglobin (iron complex), chlorophyll (magnesium complex), EDTA in water softeners and cisplatin in cancer treatment are examples of complexes in life and industry.
sla_exercise: Define a ligand.::A molecule or ion that donates a lone pair of electrons to a metal ion to form a dative covalent bond.||Find the oxidation state of cobalt in [Co(NH₃)₆]Cl₃.::NH₃ is neutral and the complex ion has a charge of +3, so Co is +3.||Give the coordination number and shape of [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺.::Coordination number 2 and linear.

sla_notes_intro: Complexes take part in ligand substitution, precipitation and redox reactions that can be observed by colour changes.
sla_notes_details: Ligand exchange: adding excess ammonia to copper(II) sulphate first gives a pale blue precipitate of Cu(OH)₂ and then a deep blue solution of [Cu(NH₃)₄(H₂O)₂]²⁺; adding concentrated HCl to [Cu(H₂O)₆]²⁺ gives yellow-green [CuCl₄]²⁻. Iron(III) ions form a blood-red complex [Fe(SCN)(H₂O)₅]²⁺ with thiocyanate, used as a test. Silver chloride dissolves in dilute ammonia forming [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺, which is the basis of Tollens' reagent. Nickel(II) forms a red precipitate with dimethylglyoxime. Stability constants describe the extent of complex formation, and the chelate effect makes complexes with polydentate ligands very stable because of an entropy increase. Experiments should be planned with small quantities, observations recorded and reported with balanced equations.
sla_notes_illustrations: Cu²⁺(aq) + 4NH₃(aq) → [Cu(NH₃)₄]²⁺(aq) (pale blue to deep blue). AgCl(s) + 2NH₃(aq) → [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) shows the dissolving of a white precipitate.
sla_notes_daily_life: Photography developing with thiosulphate, water softening using EDTA, and detection of iron or nickel in analysis all involve complex-forming reactions.
sla_exercise: What colour change is seen when excess ammonia is added to copper(II) sulphate solution?::A pale blue precipitate forms first and then dissolves to give a deep blue solution.||Which reagent gives a blood-red colour with Fe³⁺?::Thiocyanate ions (SCN⁻).||Why is EDTA used to remove hardness from water?::It forms very stable chelate complexes with Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ ions, preventing them from forming scum.

sla_notes_intro: The special properties of transition elements make them essential in industry, technology and daily life.
sla_notes_details: Copper is an excellent electrical conductor used in wiring and motors; iron and steel (alloyed with carbon, chromium, nickel and manganese) are used in construction and tools; stainless steel resists corrosion. Catalysts include iron (Haber process), vanadium(V) oxide (Contact process), nickel (hydrogenation of oils to make margarine) and platinum, palladium and rhodium in catalytic converters that convert CO, NOx and hydrocarbons to CO₂, N₂ and H₂O. Alloys such as brass (Cu and Zn), bronze (Cu and Sn) and nichrome are used for ornaments and heating elements. Titanium is used for lightweight aircraft parts and implants; chromium and gold are used for plating and jewellery. Complex compounds are used in medicine (cisplatin), in analysis, in dyes and pigments and in solar cells and photography.
sla_notes_illustrations: Adding a little manganese to steel makes it tough for railway lines, and 18/8 stainless steel contains 18% chromium and 8% nickel, giving a protective Cr₂O₃ layer that resists rusting.
sla_notes_daily_life: Electric wires, cooking pots, cars with catalytic converters, jewellery and coins, margarine and cancer treatment are examples of uses of transition elements and their complexes.
sla_exercise: State the catalyst used in the hydrogenation of vegetable oils.::Nickel.||Why is copper widely used for electric wires?::It is an excellent conductor of electricity, ductile and fairly resistant to corrosion.||What is the function of a catalytic converter?::It converts CO, oxides of nitrogen and unburnt hydrocarbons into CO₂, N₂ and H₂O using platinum group metals.

sla_notes_intro: Chemical kinetics studies how fast reactions occur and the factors that affect their rates.
sla_notes_details: The rate is the change in concentration per unit time. For aA + bB → products, rate = k[A]^m[B]^n, where m and n are orders found by experiments (not from the equation), and the overall order is m + n; k is the rate constant. Zero-order, first-order and second-order reactions are recognised by graphs: for first order ln[A] against t is linear with gradient -k and half-life t½ = 0.693/k. The initial rates method compares experiments in which one concentration is changed at a time. Collision theory says that only collisions with energy at least the activation energy Ea and with correct orientation lead to reaction. The Arrhenius equation k = Ae^(-Ea/RT) and ln k = ln A - Ea/RT show that raising temperature increases k, and a plot of ln k against 1/T gives a straight line with gradient -Ea/R. A catalyst provides an alternative route with a lower Ea. Reaction mechanisms have a slowest rate-determining step.
sla_notes_illustrations: In the experiments [A] doubled and rate doubled while [B] doubled and rate quadrupled, so rate = k[A][B]². If k for a first-order reaction is 0.0231 min⁻¹, the half-life is 30 min. A 10 °C rise typically doubles the rate because many more molecules exceed Ea.
sla_notes_daily_life: Milk goes sour faster in a warm room, food cooks quicker in a pressure cooker and enzymes in the body speed up digestion.
sla_exercise: Define order of reaction.::The sum of the powers to which concentrations are raised in the experimentally determined rate equation.||Write the relationship between half-life and rate constant for a first-order reaction.::t½ = 0.693/k.||Explain how a catalyst increases the reaction rate.::It provides an alternative reaction path with a lower activation energy, so more collisions are successful.

sla_notes_intro: Knowledge of reaction rates helps industries to produce faster, safer and cheaper, and helps in medicine and food storage.
sla_notes_details: In industry, catalysts such as iron (Haber), V₂O₅ (Contact) and enzymes in fermentation and detergents reduce the energy and cost of production. Rate control by temperature, concentration, pressure and surface area is applied in reactors, for example finely divided solids react faster because more surface area is exposed. In medicine, the rate of drug metabolism follows first-order kinetics with half-lives that decide dosing intervals (paracetamol about 2 hours), and slow-release tablets control the rate of drug release. In baking, the rate of CO₂ release from baking powder or yeast at oven temperature makes bread rise. Food storage in refrigerators and freezers slows spoilage reactions because k decreases as temperature falls, and preservatives such as antioxidants slow oxidation. Nuclear and radioactive decay also follows first-order kinetics and is used in dating.
sla_notes_illustrations: If a drug has a half-life of 4 hours, after 12 hours 1/8 of the dose remains. Storing milk at 4 °C instead of 30 °C slows bacterial reactions so much that the shelf life extends from about 1 day to about a week.
sla_notes_daily_life: Preserving food in fridges, timing medicine doses, baking bread, using enzyme detergents and controlling corrosion or fire spread use kinetics.
sla_exercise: Why does powdered marble react faster with acid than marble chips?::Powder has a larger surface area, so there are more collisions per unit time.||A drug has a half-life of 6 hours. What fraction remains after 18 hours?::Three half-lives have passed, so (1/2)³ = 1/8.||How does refrigeration preserve food?::Low temperature lowers the rate constant, so the reactions of spoilage and the growth of microorganisms are slowed.

sla_notes_intro: Electrochemistry links chemical reactions to electrical energy in galvanic and electrolytic cells.
sla_notes_details: In a galvanic cell oxidation occurs at the anode (negative) and reduction at the cathode (positive); electrons flow through the external circuit and ions move through a salt bridge. A cell diagram is written with the anode on the left and the cathode on the right, separated by a salt bridge, for example Zn(s), Zn²⁺(aq), then Cu²⁺(aq), Cu(s). Standard electrode potentials E° are measured relative to the standard hydrogen electrode (0.00 V) at 1 mol/dm³, 100 kPa and 298 K; E°cell = E°cathode - E°anode, and a positive E°cell means a spontaneous reaction. The Nernst equation E = E° - (0.0592/n) log Q at 25 °C shows the effect of concentration. Relationships: ΔG° = -nFE°cell and ΔG° = -RT ln K, where F = 96 500 C/mol. In electrolysis, Faraday's laws give m = (M x I x t)/(n x F). Cells include the Daniell cell, dry cell, lead-acid accumulator, lithium-ion and fuel cells.
sla_notes_illustrations: For the zinc-copper cell, E°cell = +0.34 - (-0.76) = +1.10 V. Passing 2.0 A for 30 minutes deposits m = 63.5 x 2.0 x 1800/(2 x 96 500) = 1.18 g of copper.
sla_notes_daily_life: Batteries in phones, torches and cars, electroplating of jewellery and taps, and the anodising of aluminium use electrochemistry.
sla_exercise: Define the standard electrode potential.::The e.m.f. of a half-cell measured against the standard hydrogen electrode under standard conditions (1 mol/dm³, 298 K, 100 kPa).||Calculate E°cell for a magnesium-silver cell (E°Mg = -2.37 V, E°Ag = +0.80 V).::E°cell = 0.80 - (-2.37) = +3.17 V.||Which charge is needed to deposit 1 mol of copper from Cu²⁺?::Two moles of electrons, 2 x 96 500 = 193 000 C.

sla_notes_intro: Electrochemical principles are applied in the protection of metals, extraction and purification of metals and the production of batteries.
sla_notes_details: Corrosion of iron is an electrochemical process in which iron is oxidised at the anode (Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻) and oxygen reduced at the cathode in the presence of water; rust is hydrated iron(III) oxide, Fe₂O₃.xH₂O. It is inhibited by painting, galvanising with zinc, oil and grease, alloying to make stainless steel, sacrificial protection with magnesium or zinc blocks, and cathodic protection of pipes. Copper is purified by electrolysis using impure copper as the anode and pure copper as the cathode in CuSO₄ solution, and aluminium is extracted by electrolysis of alumina in molten cryolite. Sodium and chlorine are made by electrolysis of brine or molten NaCl. Primary batteries (dry cells) cannot be recharged, while secondary batteries (lead-acid, lithium-ion) can, and fuel cells produce electricity from hydrogen and oxygen with water as the only product. Electroplating coats objects with a thin layer of metal such as chromium, nickel, silver or gold.
sla_notes_illustrations: In a lead-acid battery, Pb + PbO₂ + 2H₂SO₄ → 2PbSO₄ + 2H₂O gives 2.0 V per cell, and six cells in series provide 12 V for a car. A galvanised roofing sheet stays protected even when scratched because zinc corrodes in preference to iron.
sla_notes_daily_life: Painted bridges, galvanised roofing sheets, car batteries, phone batteries, plated jewellery and refined copper for cables show electrochemistry in daily life.
sla_exercise: Name the substances necessary for iron to rust.::Oxygen (air) and water.||Explain sacrificial protection.::A more reactive metal such as zinc or magnesium is attached to iron and corrodes instead of the iron.||Describe the electrodes used in refining copper.::The anode is impure copper and the cathode is pure copper in a copper(II) sulphate electrolyte.

sla_notes_intro: The project started in Form Five is finished by completing experiments, analysing data and writing a scientific report for assessment.
sla_notes_details: Students complete their experiments or product tests, repeat measurements, analyse the data with tables and graphs, calculate yields or concentrations with uncertainties, and compare them with expectations or standards. The report is structured as a title page, abstract, acknowledgements, table of contents, introduction and objectives, literature review, methodology, results and analysis, discussion, conclusion, recommendations, references and appendices. Safety, ethics and honesty in reporting are emphasised, and sources are cited using a standard format. The product or findings may be displayed at a science exhibition, and the assessment covers planning, procedure, results, communication and the quality of the product.
sla_notes_illustrations: A group that produced liquid soap from local oil reports the pH (9.5), foaming test, cleaning efficiency and cost per litre, then compares their product with a commercial soap and recommends improvements such as adding a colourant and a preservative.
sla_notes_daily_life: Producing goods such as soap, natural dyes or water purifiers from a school project can lead to small enterprises that serve the community.
sla_exercise: List the main parts of a scientific project report.::Abstract, introduction, methodology, results, discussion, conclusion and references.||Why should results be compared with a standard or literature values?::To judge the quality and validity of the product or findings.||What is the purpose of the recommendations section?::To suggest how the work can be improved, applied or continued.
